2.text: inside of the outer room, even while cooking is going on, is almost the same

3.text: as that outside. The herdsmen or hunters, when sleeping in the open, although

4.text: they may have an abundance of fuel, are often content to make a small

5.text: smouldering fire from which to light their pipes, or do not make any fire;

6.text: whereas the Lamut and the Yukaghir send up a blaze that wards off the

7.text: cold from a space of several yards around, and often keep it up during the

8.text: whole night in order to get a chance to sleep comfortably.

9.text: Movable House. — The type of tent and sleeping-room here described

10.text: is especially used in moving about with the herd. That used by the family

11.text: is very heavy, and requires — with poles, cover, and bedding — six or seven

12.text: sledges. Whenever the herdsmen leave their principal camp, they carry with

13.text: them a small sleeping-room, with a light tent, which is often not properly

14.text: pitched, but only loosely thrown over the sleeping-room to keep off the

15.text: snow. In this type of house it is difficult to dry damp clothing. Fur clothing

16.text: generally becomes damp quickly, even in dry, cold weather, especially when

17.text: it is worn directly on the skin, without any underclothing. When damp, it

18.text: does not protect the body from the cold: therefore it must be dried every

19.text: night while its owner is asleep. In the sleeping-room of the Reindeer Chukchee

20.text: the only place for drying things is directly over the lamp. Only small articles,

21.text: such as mittens, socks, and boots, can be placed there. Large pieces of

22.text: clothing, such as shirt or trousers, are dried in a way similar to that used

23.text: in drying the sleeping-room cover; i. e., by freezing the dampness out, then

24.text: shaking it off with the snow-beater, and finally drying for a long time in

25.text: the cold dry wind. The Chukchee herdsman sometimes walks for a fortnight

26.text: in damp clothes without a chance to dry them, and takes off his undershirt

27.text: only when it is quite spoiled and unfit for further use. On this account the

28.text: Reindeer Chukchee are always anxious to avoid the damp. For instance,

29.text: before coming into the inner room, the whole dress, from the cap to the

30.text: shaggy boot-soles, is well beaten with the beater to remove the slightest

31.text: trace of snow, which otherwise would melt in the warm interior and cause

32.text: additional trouble. In the evening, when the sleeping-tents are put in place

33.text: ready for occupancy, the entire camp begins to resound on all sides with the

34.text: short rapping of the snow-beaters, which lasts for half an hour before all the

35.text: people are ready to retire. Travellers and herdsmen often have beaters of

36.text: their own, which are carried on the belt or are attached to the sledge-grating.

37.text: The snow-beaters for clothing (Fig. 98) are more slender than those used

38.text: for the room-covers. The knob is often fashioned in the shape of a human

39.text: or dog’s head, which then plays the role of the protecting spirit, the so-called
